questions.question: Which of the following aqueous solutions should have the highest boiling point?
questions.answer:
**(B)** 1·0 M Na$_2$SO$_4$

Elevation of boiling point is colligative, so it depends on the **total number of ions** in solution:

$$\Delta T_b=iK_bm$$

All four solutions have the same molarity, so the one with the largest van't Hoff factor $i$ boils highest. Na$_2$SO$_4$ gives **three ions** ($2\ce{Na+}+\ce{SO4^{2-}}$, $i\approx3$), while NaOH ($i\approx2$), NH$_4$NO$_3$ ($i=2$) and KNO$_3$ ($i=2$) each give two. So the sulphate solution has the highest boiling point.

questions.question: An example of colligative property of solution is
questions.answer:
**(C)** elevation of boiling point

Colligative properties depend only on the **number of solute particles**, not on their identity: relative lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point and osmotic pressure. Density, mass and temperature are ordinary physical properties of the solution, not colligative ones.

questions.question: What is the molarity of a solution with a mass of solute 10 kg mass and 100 litre volume?
questions.answer:
**(A)** 0·1 molar *(as keyed — see note)*

Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution:

$$M=\frac{n}{V}=\frac{\text{mass}/M_2}{V}$$

With the data exactly as printed (10 kg of solute in 100 L), if the solute were, say, NaOH ($M=40$):

$$M=\frac{10000/40}{100}=2.5\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

so the answer depends entirely on the molar mass, which the question does not give.

*Note on the printed key:* the key marks (A) 0·1 molar, which corresponds to **1 kg (not 10 kg)** of a solute of molar mass 100 g mol$^{-1}$ in 100 L — i.e. the stem's '10 kg' appears to be a misprint. As printed, the question cannot be answered without the molar mass; the keyed answer 0·1 M is recorded here for completeness.

questions.question: The unit of molar conductivity is
questions.answer:
**(B)** S cm$^{2}$mol$^{-1}$

Molar conductivity is conductivity divided by molar concentration:

$$\Lambda_m=\frac{\kappa}{c}=\frac{\text{S cm}^{-1}}{\text{mol cm}^{-3}}=\text{S cm}^{2}\text{mol}^{-1}$$

(When $c$ is in mol m$^{-3}$ the unit is S m$^{2}$ mol$^{-1}$; the two differ by a factor of $10^{4}$.)

questions.question: The amount of electricity required to obtain one mole of Zn from ZnSO$_4$ solution will be
questions.answer:
**(D)** 2F

Zinc is deposited from ZnSO$_4$ as

$$\ce{Zn^{2+} + 2e^- -> Zn}$$

Two moles of electrons — i.e. **2 faraday** (2 × 96500 = 193000 C) — are needed per mole of zinc, because Zn$^{2+}$ requires two electrons. One faraday would give only half a mole.

questions.question: The unit of rate constant for the reaction 2H$_2$ + 2NO → 2H$_2$O + N$_2$, which has rate R = k[H$_2$][NO]$^2$ is
questions.answer:
**(C)** mol$^{-2}$ L$^{2}$ s$^{-1}$

The rate law is third order overall (one H$_2$ + two NO), so

$$k=\frac{\text{rate}}{[\ce{H2}][\ce{NO}]^2}=\frac{\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}}{(\text{mol L}^{-1})^3}=\text{mol}^{-2}\text{L}^{2}\text{s}^{-1}$$

For an $n^{th}$-order reaction the unit is mol$^{1-n}$ L$^{n-1}$ s$^{-1}$; here $n=3$.

questions.question: What is the concentration of the reactant in a first order reaction, when the rate of the reaction is 0·6 Ms$^{-1}$ and the rate constant is 0·035 s$^{-1}$?
questions.answer:
**(B)** 17·143 M

For a first-order reaction $\text{rate}=k[\ce{R}]$, so

$$[\ce{R}]=\frac{\text{rate}}{k}=\frac{0.6}{0.035}=17.14\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

**17·1 M.** The concentration comes out very large because the rate constant is large (0.035 s$^{-1}$) — a fast reaction at a high concentration.

questions.question: Which of the following represents Arrhenius equation?
questions.answer:
**(B)** $k=Ae^{-Ea/RT}$

The rate constant falls exponentially as the activation energy rises and grows steeply as temperature rises:

$$k=Ae^{-E_a/RT}$$

In logarithmic form $\log k=\log A-\dfrac{E_a}{2.303RT}$, so a plot of $\log k$ against $1/T$ is a straight line of slope $-E_a/2.303R$. Option (A) has the wrong sign — it would make the rate *fall* with temperature.

questions.question: Which of the following is a diamagnetic ion?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Sc$^{3+}$

Sc$^{3+}$ is $3d^0$ — it has **no d electrons at all**, so no unpaired electron and it is **diamagnetic** (and colourless). V$^{2+}$ is $3d^3$ (three unpaired), Cu$^{2+}$ is $3d^9$ (one unpaired) and Mn$^{2+}$ is $3d^5$ (five unpaired); all three are paramagnetic.

questions.question: Which property of transition metals enables them to behave as catalysts?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Variable oxidation state

Transition metals readily change oxidation state by gaining or losing electrons, so they can act as **electron relays** — oxidising one reactant and then being re-oxidised by another — which is exactly how a catalyst provides an alternative low-energy path. Their ability to **adsorb** reactants on the surface and to form intermediate complexes adds to this.

High melting point and alloy formation are consequences of strong metallic bonding and are irrelevant to catalysis; a high ionisation enthalpy would if anything hinder it.

questions.question: Oxidation state of Cu in [Cu(NH$_3$)$_4$]$^{2+}$ is
questions.answer:
**(C)** +2

Ammonia is a **neutral** ligand, so the charge on the metal equals the charge on the complex ion:

$$x+4(0)=+2\ \Rightarrow\ x=+2$$

Copper is present as Cu(II), $3d^9$ — one unpaired electron, hence the deep blue colour and paramagnetism of tetraamminecopper(II).

questions.question: $dsp^2$ hybridisation is present in
questions.answer:
**(B)** [Ni(CN)$_4$]$^{2-}$

In $[\ce{Ni(CN)4}]^{2-}$ the strong-field cyanide forces the $3d^8$ electrons of Ni(II) to pair up, freeing one 3d orbital; the complex is then formed by **$dsp^2$** hybridisation and is **square planar and diamagnetic (low spin)**.

By contrast $[\ce{Ni(CO)4}]$ is $sp^3$ **tetrahedral** (Ni(0), $3d^{10}$), $[\ce{Cu(NH3)4}]^{2+}$ is square planar but $sp^2d$ in some treatments, and $[\ce{MnCl4}]^{2-}$ is $sp^3$ tetrahedral.

questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of the following compound? CH$_3$—CH=CH—CH$_2$Br
questions.answer:
**(C)** 1-Bromobut-2-ene

The chain has four carbons with a double bond between C-2 and C-3 and the bromine on C-1:

$$\ce{BrCH2-CH=CH-CH3}$$

Numbering from the bromine end gives the double bond the lower locant (2 rather than 2 from the other end but bromo at C-4). So the name is **1-bromobut-2-ene**.

*Note on the printed key:* the paper has ticks against **both** (C) and (D). (D) 4-bromobut-2-ene numbers the chain the wrong way round (giving bromine locant 4 instead of 1), so (C) is the correct IUPAC name.

questions.question: In which medium does Finkelstein reaction take place?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Dry acetone

The **Finkelstein reaction** is the exchange of an alkyl chloride or bromide for the iodide using NaI:

$$\ce{R-Cl + NaI ->[\text{dry acetone}] R-I + NaCl v}$$

The medium must be **dry acetone** because NaI dissolves in acetone while NaCl and NaBr do not — the precipitation of the sodium halide is what drives the equilibrium to the iodide. In water all three halides are soluble and no such driving force exists.

questions.question: The test used to distinguish between primary, secondary and tertiary alcohol is
questions.answer:
**(B)** Lucas test

The **Lucas test** uses Lucas reagent (concentrated HCl + anhydrous ZnCl$_2$). The alcohol is protonated and then displaced by chloride; the rate depends on the stability of the carbocation, so:

- **Tertiary** alcohol — immediate turbidity (3° cation, most stable).
- **Secondary** alcohol — turbidity within about 5 minutes.
- **Primary** alcohol — no turbidity at room temperature (needs heating).

Tollens' and Fehling's tests are for aldehydes; Hinsberg's reagent distinguishes classes of amines.

questions.question: Ethyl alcohol $\xrightarrow{Cu/573K}$ A, 'A' is
questions.answer:
**(A)** Acetaldehyde

Passing ethanol vapour over **copper heated to 573 K** removes hydrogen from the alcohol (dehydrogenation), giving the aldehyde:

$$\ce{CH3CH2OH ->[Cu][573 K] CH3CHO + H2}$$

Oxidation and dehydrogenation give the same product here. Further oxidation would give ethanoic acid, but that needs an oxidising agent such as acidified dichromate, not hot copper.

questions.question: Which reaction is used for the preparation of symmetric and asymmetric ethers?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Williamson synthesis

An alkoxide attacks a primary alkyl halide in an S$_N$2 displacement:

$$\ce{R-ONa + R'-X -> R-O-R' + NaX}$$

Because R and R′ can be chosen independently, both **symmetrical** ($\ce{R=R'}$) and **unsymmetrical** ethers can be made, and aryl alkyl ethers (e.g. anisole) too. (Finkelstein makes alkyl iodides, Reimer-Tiemann salicylaldehyde, Etard benzaldehyde.)

questions.question: Oxidation of propan-1-ol with alkaline KMnO$_4$ solution gives
questions.answer:
**(A)** propanoic acid

Propan-1-ol is a **primary** alcohol, so oxidation first gives the aldehyde (propanal), which is itself oxidised further because it still has a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon. With a strong oxidant such as hot alkaline KMnO$_4$ (which is reduced to green manganate) the final product is the acid:

$$\ce{CH3CH2CH2OH ->[KMnO4/OH^-] CH3CH2CHO ->[KMnO4/OH^-] CH3CH2COOH}$$

So propanoic acid (as its potassium salt in alkaline medium) is formed.

questions.question: The reaction phenol + CHCl$_3$ + KOH $\xrightarrow{\Delta}$ salicylaldehyde is
questions.answer:
**(C)** Reimer-Tiemann reaction

Phenol treated with **chloroform and aqueous/alcoholic alkali** gives **salicylaldehyde**, the —CHO entering ortho to the —OH:

$$\ce{C6H5OH + CHCl3 + 3KOH -> o-HOC6H4CHO + 3KCl + 2H2O}$$

The reactive intermediate is **dichlorocarbene**, $\ce{:CCl2}$, generated by the action of hydroxide on chloroform, which attacks the activated ring. (Gattermann-Koch formylates benzene with CO/HCl; Sandmeyer replaces a diazonium group; Fittig couples aryl halides.)

questions.question: What is the relation between acidic strength of A and B? A = o-methoxybenzoic acid, B = o-nitrobenzoic acid
questions.answer:
**(C)** A < B

Acid strength depends on the stability of the carboxylate ion. The **—NO$_2$** group of B is strongly **electron-withdrawing** ($-I$, $-M$) and, being ortho, also stabilises the anion by a close hydrogen bond/field effect, so **o-nitrobenzoic acid is much the stronger acid** ($\text{p}K_a$ ≈ 2.2).

The **—OCH$_3$** group of A is **electron-releasing** ($+M$), and in the ortho position it also disturbs the coplanarity needed for resonance in the acid, both of which **destabilise** the anion — o-methoxybenzoic acid is therefore weaker ($\text{p}K_a$ ≈ 4.1) than benzoic acid even.

So A < B.

questions.question: C$_6$H$_5$CONH$_2$ + Br$_2$ + 4NaOH → Product. Product is
questions.answer:
**(C)** C$_6$H$_5$NH$_2$

This is the **Hofmann bromamide degradation**: an amide is treated with bromine and alkali, loses its carbonyl group as carbonate, and gives a primary amine **with one carbon less**:

$$\ce{C6H5CONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH -> C6H5NH2 + Na2CO3 + 2NaBr + 2H2O}$$

Benzamide therefore gives **aniline** (benzenamine). The intermediate is N-bromobenzamide, which rearranges with migration of the phenyl group to nitrogen, then hydrolyses.

questions.question: The test which is used to distinguish between primary amine and secondary amine is
questions.answer:
**(B)** Carbylamine test

On warming with chloroform and alcoholic KOH, **primary** amines form the evil-smelling isocyanide:

$$\ce{RNH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH -> RNC + 3KCl + 3H2O}$$

A **secondary** amine has only one hydrogen on nitrogen and cannot give this reaction, so the carbylamine test cleanly distinguishes 1° from 2° (and 3°) amines. Lucas' reagent distinguishes alcohols and Tollens'/Fehling's distinguish aldehydes.

questions.question: Which of the following monosaccharides is a ketohexose?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Fructose

**Fructose**, $\ce{C6H12O6}$, has a **ketone** group at C-2 (a ketohexose); glucose, galactose and mannose are all **aldohexoses**, with an aldehyde at C-1. In its cyclic form fructose is a five-membered **fructofuranose**, which is why sucrose (glucose + fructose) is a non-reducing sugar with an $\alpha$-1,2 linkage.

questions.question: Identify the complementary strand of the DNA primary structure ATGCCGATC.
questions.answer:
**(B)** TACGGCTAG

Base pairing in DNA is A–T and G–C, and the strands are antiparallel. Taking the complement base by base:

$$\ce{A\to T,\ T\to A,\ G\to C,\ C\to G,\ C\to G,\ G\to C,\ A\to T,\ T\to A,\ C\to G}$$

$$\text{ATGCCGATC}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{TACGGCTAG}$$

Option (A) uses uracil and so would be an RNA copy; (D) is the same strand reversed rather than complemented. *(The printed option (B) reads 'TACGGCJAG' — an OCR/typing slip for TACGGCTAG.)*

questions.question: Retinol is vitamin
questions.answer:
**(A)** A

**Retinol is vitamin A** — a fat-soluble alcohol obtained from fish-liver oils, liver, butter and egg yolk (and from $\beta$-carotene in carrots and green vegetables). It is the precursor of **rhodopsin**, the visual pigment, so its deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia, and it is also needed for healthy epithelia and growth.

questions.question: State Henry's law.
questions.answer:
**Henry's law:** at constant temperature, the **solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of the gas above the liquid**:

$$p=K_H\,x$$

where $p$ is the partial pressure of the gas, $x$ its mole fraction in the solution and $K_H$ the Henry's law constant (a characteristic of the gas–solvent pair at that temperature). Equivalently the mass of gas dissolved per unit volume is proportional to its pressure.

Consequences: gases are more soluble at high pressure (why soda is bottled under CO$_2$ pressure) and less soluble at high temperature (why warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, and why boiling removes dissolved air).

questions.question: Predict the order of the reaction in the given plot. (A graph of $t_{1/2}$ against $[R_0]$ is a horizontal straight line.)
questions.answer:
**The reaction is first order.**

For a first-order reaction

$$t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{k}$$

which contains **no concentration term at all** — the half-life is a constant, independent of the initial concentration. A plot of $t_{1/2}$ against $[R_0]$ is therefore a **horizontal line**.

(For comparison, a zero-order reaction gives $t_{1/2}=\dfrac{[R_0]}{2k}$, a straight line through the origin, and a second-order reaction gives $t_{1/2}=\dfrac{1}{k[R_0]}$, a hyperbola.)

questions.question: Write the electronic configuration of Cr$^{3+}$ (Z = 24).
questions.answer:
Chromium is $[\ce{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^1$ (the anomalous configuration that gives a half-filled d subshell). Removing three electrons — the 4s electron first, then two 3d electrons — leaves

$$\ce{Cr^{3+}}:\ [\ce{Ar}]\,3d^3$$

or in full

$$1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,3d^3$$

With three unpaired d electrons ($\uparrow\ \uparrow\ \uparrow$) Cr$^{3+}$ is **paramagnetic**, $\mu=\sqrt{3\times5}=3.87$ B.M., and it is coloured (violet in aqueous solution as $[\ce{Cr(H2O)6}]^{3+}$).

questions.question: What type of isomerism is shown by the complex [Co(NH$_3$)$_6$][Cr(CN)$_6$]?
questions.answer:
**Coordination (ionisation) isomerism** — specifically **coordination isomerism**.

The cation and the anion are both complex ions, and the ligands can be distributed differently between the two metals. The isomer of the same molecular formula is

$$\ce{[Cr(NH3)6][Co(CN)6]}$$

In one compound cobalt carries the ammine ligands and chromium the cyanides; in the other the metals are exchanged. The two differ in their properties (colour, solubility, reactivity) because the metals are in different ligand environments. This type of isomerism is possible only when **both** the cation and the anion are complex.

questions.question: Write the structure of the product when Butan-2-ol reacts with CrO$_3$.
questions.answer:
Butan-2-ol is a **secondary** alcohol, so oxidation (Jones reagent, CrO$_3$ in aqueous acid) removes the hydrogen on the carbinol carbon and gives a **ketone**:

$$\ce{CH3CH2CH(OH)CH3 ->[CrO3][H^+] CH3CH2COCH3 + H2O}$$

The product is **butan-2-one (methyl ethyl ketone)**:

$$\ce{CH3-CO-CH2-CH3}$$

It cannot be oxidised further, because the carbonyl carbon carries no hydrogen.

questions.question: Name the reagent which is used to convert aldehydes or ketones having α-hydrogen into β hydroxy aldehydes or β-hydroxy ketones.
questions.answer:
**Dilute aqueous alkali** — dilute NaOH (or dilute KOH, or barium hydroxide) — used in the **aldol condensation**.

The base removes the acidic $\alpha$-hydrogen of one molecule to form a carbanion (enolate), which attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second molecule:

$$\ce{CH3CHO + CH3CHO ->[dil. NaOH] CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO}$$

The product, a $\beta$-hydroxy aldehyde ('aldol') or $\beta$-hydroxy ketone, loses water on warming to give an $\alpha$,$\beta$-unsaturated carbonyl compound.

questions.question: What happens when aniline is treated with bromine water?
questions.answer:
Aniline gives an **immediate white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline**:

$$\ce{C6H5NH2 + 3Br2(aq) -> 2,4,6-Br3C6H2NH2 v + 3HBr}$$

The —NH$_2$ group is strongly **activating and ortho/para directing**, so the ring is brominated at all three available positions **without any Lewis-acid catalyst** — a dramatic illustration of how strongly the amino group activates the ring. With bromine in CS$_2$ at low temperature the reaction stops at the monobromo stage (p-bromoaniline).

questions.question: Proteins are polymers of what?
questions.answer:
**Proteins are polymers of amino acids** — specifically $\alpha$-amino acids, joined by **peptide bonds** ($\ce{-CO-NH-}$):

$$\ce{H2N-CH(R)-COOH + H2N-CH(R')-COOH -> H2N-CH(R)-CO-NH-CH(R')-COOH + H2O}$$

The sequence of amino acids (the primary structure) is dictated by DNA; the chain then folds into secondary structures ($\alpha$-helix, $\beta$-sheet) held by hydrogen bonds, and into a tertiary three-dimensional shape. There are about 20 standard amino acids, and on complete hydrolysis a protein yields only these.

questions.question: Which vitamin helps in blood clotting?
questions.answer:
**Vitamin K** (phylloquinone/menaquinone).

The liver requires vitamin K as a cofactor for the carboxylation of glutamic acid residues in **prothrombin** and several other clotting factors (VII, IX, X), which is what allows them to bind calcium and take part in the clotting cascade. Its deficiency therefore causes prolonged clotting time, bleeding gums and, in the newborn, haemorrhagic disease.

questions.question: Write the reactions of Fuel cell.
questions.answer:
A **hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell** converts the chemical energy of combustion directly into electricity, with about 70% efficiency (far better than a heat engine). The electrodes are porous carbon containing a catalyst, with concentrated KOH or NaOH as electrolyte.

**Anode (oxidation of hydrogen):**

$$\ce{2H2(g) + 4OH^-(aq) -> 4H2O(l) + 4e^-}$$

**Cathode (reduction of oxygen):**

$$\ce{O2(g) + 2H2O(l) + 4e^- -> 4OH^-(aq)}$$

**Overall cell reaction:**

$$\ce{2H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2H2O(l)}$$

The only product is water, so the cell is non-polluting. The emf is about 1.23 V (practically ~0.9 V), and the cell runs continuously as long as hydrogen and oxygen are supplied — it does not need recharging. Fuel cells power spacecraft (Apollo, Gemini) and are being developed for vehicles.

questions.question: In the following ions — Sc$^{3+}$ (Z = 21), V$^{3+}$ (Z = 23), Mn$^{2+}$ (Z = 25), Co$^{2+}$ (Z = 27), Cu$^{+}$ (Z = 29) — (a) which is/are colourless? (b) which is/are paramagnetic? (c) which has maximum number of unpaired electrons?
questions.answer:
First write the d configurations:

| Ion | Configuration | Unpaired e$^-$ |
|---|---|---|
| Sc$^{3+}$ | $3d^0$ | 0 |
| V$^{3+}$ | $3d^2$ | 2 |
| Mn$^{2+}$ | $3d^5$ | 5 |
| Co$^{2+}$ | $3d^7$ | 3 |
| Cu$^+$ | $3d^{10}$ | 0 |

**(a) Colourless:** an ion is colourless when it has no incomplete d subshell to allow a $d$–$d$ transition — so **Sc$^{3+}$ ($3d^0$) and Cu$^+$ ($3d^{10}$)**.

**(b) Paramagnetic:** an ion is paramagnetic when it has one or more unpaired electrons — so **V$^{3+}$, Mn$^{2+}$ and Co$^{2+}$** (Sc$^{3+}$ and Cu$^+$ are diamagnetic).

**(c) Maximum unpaired electrons: Mn$^{2+}$**, with a **half-filled $3d^5$** configuration — five unpaired electrons, giving the largest spin-only moment of the set:

$$\mu=\sqrt{5(5+2)}=\sqrt{35}=5.92\ \text{B.M.}$$

(for comparison V$^{3+}$ 3.87, Co$^{2+}$ 3.87 B.M.).

questions.question: Zn, Cd and Hg are not considered as transition elements. Explain giving reason.
questions.answer:
A **transition element** is defined as a d-block element whose atom or common ion has an **incompletely filled d subshell** in the ground state, so that it can show the characteristic properties — variable oxidation state, $d$–$d$ transitions (colour), paramagnetism and catalytic activity.

Zn, Cd and Hg have the configurations

$$\ce{Zn}: [\ce{Ar}]\,3d^{10}4s^2,\qquad \ce{Cd}: [\ce{Kr}]\,4d^{10}5s^2,\qquad \ce{Hg}: [\ce{Xe}]\,4f^{14}5d^{10}6s^2$$

Each has a **completely filled d subshell** in the ground state, and the only common oxidation state — **+2** — also leaves the d subshell full ($d^{10}$). Therefore:

1. They show **only one oxidation state** (+2) in their compounds.
2. There can be **no $d$–$d$ transition**, so all their compounds are **colourless or white** (ZnO white, ZnSO$_4$ white).
3. They are **diamagnetic**, because all electrons are paired.
4. Their ions are not effective catalysts in the way transition-metal ions are.

For these reasons Zn, Cd and Hg are d-block elements but **not transition elements**.

questions.question: Using IUPAC norms write the names of the following: (a) K$_3$[Cr(C$_2$O$_4$)$_3$] (b) [Co(NH$_3$)$_5$Cl]Cl$_2$ (c) [Ti(H$_2$O)$_6$]$^{3+}$
questions.answer:
**(a) K$_3$[Cr(C$_2$O$_4$)$_3$]** — three bidentate oxalato ligands with Cr(III) ($x+3(-2)=-3\Rightarrow x=+3$), balanced by three K$^+$:

**potassium trioxalatochromate(III)**

**(b) [Co(NH$_3$)$_5$Cl]Cl$_2$** — five ammine and one chlorido on Co(III), with two chlorides outside the coordination sphere:

**pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride**

The free chloride ions are ionisable; the coordinated one is not, which is why the complex gives only two moles of AgCl with AgNO$_3$.

**(c) [Ti(H$_2$O)$_6$]$^{3+}$** — six aqua ligands on Ti(III):

**hexaaquatitanium(III) ion**

This is the species responsible for the purple colour of Ti$^{3+}$ solutions, since its single $3d$ electron gives a $d$–$d$ transition.

questions.question: Complete the following: (a) bromobenzene + Mg → (b) anisole + conc. HNO$_3$/conc. H$_2$SO$_4$ → (c) $\ce{CH3CHO + NH2-NH2 ->[H^+]}$
questions.answer:
**(a)** Bromobenzene with magnesium in **dry ether** gives the Grignard reagent, phenylmagnesium bromide:

$$\ce{C6H5Br + Mg ->[\text{dry ether}] C6H5MgBr}$$

Any moisture must be excluded, since water destroys the reagent by converting it to benzene.

**(b)** Anisole (methoxybenzene) is nitrated by the mixed acid; the **—OCH$_3$ group is ortho/para directing**, and because it is bulky the para product predominates:

$$\ce{C6H5OCH3 + HNO3 ->[H2SO4] p-NO2C6H4OCH3 + o-NO2C6H4OCH3 + H2O}$$

with **p-nitroanisole** as the major product (plus some o-nitroanisole).

**(c)** Acetaldehyde condenses with hydrazine in acid to give **acetaldehyde hydrazone**:

$$\ce{CH3CHO + H2N-NH2 ->[H^+] CH3CH=N-NH2 + H2O}$$

The reaction is acid-catalysed (pH ≈ 4.5 is optimum) because the acid protonates the carbonyl oxygen, making it more electrophilic.

questions.question: How will you bring about the following conversions? (a) Chloroethane to butane (b) Cyclohexanol to cyclohexanone (c) Benzene diazonium chloride to chlorobenzene
questions.answer:
**(a) Chloroethane → butane:** the **Wurtz reaction** — coupling of two molecules of the alkyl halide with sodium in dry ether:

$$\ce{2CH3CH2Cl + 2Na ->[\text{dry ether}] CH3CH2CH2CH3 + 2NaCl}$$

The chain doubles from two to four carbons.

**(b) Cyclohexanol → cyclohexanone:** oxidation of the secondary alcohol with acidified dichromate (or CrO$_3$/Jones reagent, or hot alkaline KMnO$_4$):

$$\ce{C6H11OH ->[K2Cr2O7/H2SO4] C6H10O + H2O}$$

The product is cyclohexanone, the ketone — it cannot be oxidised further.

**(c) Benzenediazonium chloride → chlorobenzene:** the **Sandmeyer reaction** with copper(I) chloride in hydrochloric acid:

$$\ce{C6H5N2^+Cl^- + CuCl/HCl -> C6H5Cl + N2 ^ + CuCl2}$$

(Copper powder with HCl — the Gattermann variant — gives the same product.)

questions.question: Write the IUPAC names of following compounds: (a) CH$_3$CH=CHC(Br)(CH$_3$)$_2$ (b) C$_6$H$_5$OC$_2$H$_5$ (c) m-BrC$_6$H$_4$NH$_2$
questions.answer:
**(a) $\ce{CH3CH=CHC(Br)(CH3)2}$** — a five-carbon chain with the double bond between C-3 and C-4 and the bromine and a methyl on C-2, numbering from the right so that the double bond gets the lower locant:

$$\ce{(CH3)2C(Br)-CH=CH-CH3}$$

**2-bromo-2-methylpent-3-ene**

**(b) $\ce{C6H5OC2H5}$** — an ethoxy group on a benzene ring:

**ethoxybenzene** (trivial name: phenetole). It is an aryl alkyl ether, best made by the Williamson synthesis from sodium phenoxide and ethyl bromide.

**(c) $\ce{m-BrC6H4NH2}$** — 3-bromoaniline: the amino group at C-1 fixes the numbering and bromine is at the meta position (C-3):

**3-bromoaniline**

questions.question: Differentiate between fibrous protein and globular protein.
questions.answer:
| Fibrous proteins | Globular proteins |
|---|---|
| Polypeptide chains lie **side by side in long threads or sheets** | Chains are **coiled into compact, roughly spherical** shapes |
| Held by intermolecular hydrogen bonds and **disulphide bridges between chains** | Held by hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions and hydrophobic effects within one chain |
| **Insoluble in water** | **Soluble in water** |
| Structural and contractile role | Functional role — enzymes, hormones, transport |
| Examples: **keratin, collagen, myosin, fibrin** | Examples: **insulin, albumin, haemoglobin, enzyme lysozyme** |

So fibrous proteins give mechanical strength (hair, tendon, muscle) while globular proteins carry out the chemistry of the cell.

questions.question: A 5% solution (by mass) of cane sugar in water has freezing point of 271 K. Calculate the freezing point of 5% glucose in water if freezing point of pure water is 273·15 K.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — find $K_f$ of water from the sucrose data.**

A 5% solution means 5 g of sucrose in 95 g of water. Molar mass of sucrose $\ce{C12H22O11}=342\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$:

$$n=\frac{5}{342}=0.01462\ \text{mol},\qquad \text{molality}=\frac{0.01462}{0.095}=0.1539\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$$

The observed depression is $273.15-271=2.15$ K, so

$$K_f=\frac{\Delta T_f}{m}=\frac{2.15}{0.1539}=13.97\ \text{K kg mol}^{-1}$$

*(Note: this value is far larger than the tabulated $K_f$ for water, 1.86 K kg mol$^{-1}$, which would give a depression of only 0.29 K for this solution. The calculation below uses the value implied by the paper's data, which is what the question asks for.)*

**Step 2 — apply it to glucose.** 5% glucose means 5 g in 95 g of water; $M(\ce{C6H12O6})=180$:

$$n=\frac{5}{180}=0.02778\ \text{mol},\qquad m=\frac{0.02778}{0.095}=0.2924\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$$

$$\Delta T_f=K_fm=13.97\times0.2924=4.09\ \text{K}$$

$$T_f=273.15-4.09=269.06\ \text{K}$$

**The 5% glucose solution freezes at about 269.1 K.**

The ratio of the two depressions is simply the ratio of the molalities, since $K_f$ cancels:

$$\frac{\Delta T_f(\text{glucose})}{\Delta T_f(\text{sucrose})}=\frac{M_{\text{sucrose}}}{M_{\text{glucose}}}=\frac{342}{180}=1.90$$

so $\Delta T_f=1.90\times2.15=4.09$ K — the same answer without needing $K_f$ at all. (With the correct $K_f=1.86$ the two depressions would be 0.286 K and 0.544 K, giving a freezing point of 272.6 K.)

questions.question: Calculate the emf of the following cell at 298 K: Cr(s) | Cr$^{3+}$(0.1M) || Fe$^{2+}$(0.01M) | Fe(s). (Given $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}=+0.30$ V)
questions.answer:
The cell reaction is

$$\ce{2Cr(s) + 3Fe^{2+} -> 2Cr^{3+} + 3Fe(s)}$$

so **$n=6$** electrons are transferred (2 × 3 = 3 × 2).

By the Nernst equation:

$$E=E^\circ-\frac{0.0591}{n}\log\frac{[\ce{Cr^{3+}}]^2}{[\ce{Fe^{2+}}]^3}$$

With $[\ce{Cr^{3+}}]=0.1$ M and $[\ce{Fe^{2+}}]=0.01$ M:

$$\frac{(0.1)^2}{(0.01)^3}=\frac{10^{-2}}{10^{-6}}=10^{4}$$

$$\log10^{4}=4$$

$$E=0.30-\frac{0.0591}{6}\times4=0.30-0.00985\times4=0.30-0.0394$$

$$E=+0.2606\ \text{V}\approx0.26\ \text{V}$$

**The emf of the cell is 0.26 V.**

Since the anode compartment has the *higher* ion concentration and the cathode the lower, the cell emf is **below** the standard value — a build-up of Cr$^{3+}$ and dilution of Fe$^{2+}$ both oppose the forward reaction, exactly as Le Chatelier's principle predicts.

questions.question: (a) Mention any two factors affecting rate of reaction. (b) Distinguish between order and molecularity of a reaction.
questions.answer:
**(a) Factors affecting the rate.**

1. **Concentration of reactants** (and, for a heterogeneous reaction, the **surface area** of the solid). Rate is proportional to the collision frequency, which rises with concentration; a powdered solid reacts much faster than a lump.
2. **Temperature.** The rate rises steeply — roughly doubling or tripling per 10 K — because the fraction of molecules with energy above $E_a$ increases exponentially, $k=Ae^{-E_a/RT}$.
3. *(Others: presence of a catalyst, which lowers $E_a$; presence and intensity of light for photochemical reactions.)*

**(b) Order vs molecularity.**

| Order | Molecularity |
|---|---|
| Sum of the powers of the concentration terms in the **experimentally determined rate law** | Number of species colliding simultaneously in an **elementary step** |
| Determined **experimentally** | Derived from the **mechanism** — theoretical |
| May be zero, integral or **fractional** | Always a **whole number** (1, 2, 3) |
| Defined for complex reactions as well as elementary ones | Defined only for elementary reactions |
| Can be zero | Cannot be zero |

For example, the hydrolysis of an ester in water is first order in ester but bimolecular in its elementary step; and $\ce{H2 + Cl2 ->[h\nu] 2HCl}$ is zero order although its molecularity is 2.

questions.question: On the basis of Valence Bond Theory discuss the geometric and magnetic properties of K$_4$[Fe(CN)$_6$].
questions.answer:
**Oxidation state.** With four K$^+$ and six CN$^-$:

$$x+6(-1)=-4\ \Rightarrow\ x=+2$$

so the metal is **Fe(II)**, $3d^6$.

**Hybridisation.** Cyanide is a **strong-field ligand**, so the six d electrons of Fe$^{2+}$ are forced to pair up into three of the $3d$ orbitals ($t_{2g}$):

$$3d: \uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\downarrow\ \ \_\ \ \_$$

Pairing frees **two 3d orbitals**, which then mix with one 4s and three 4p orbitals to give **$d^2sp^3$ (inner-orbital) hybridisation**.

**Geometry.** Six $d^2sp^3$ hybrid orbitals point to the corners of a regular **octahedron**, so $[\ce{Fe(CN)6}]^{4-}$ is **octahedral** with all Fe–C–N bonds equivalent (bond angle 90°).

**Magnetic properties.** All six d electrons are **paired**, so there is **no unpaired electron**:

$$n=0\ \Rightarrow\ \mu=0\ \text{B.M.}$$

The complex is **diamagnetic** and constitutes a **low-spin** complex. Its colour (pale yellow) comes from a charge-transfer transition, not a $d$–$d$ transition, since a $d^6$ low-spin ion has no spin-allowed $d$–$d$ absorption.

The outer-orbital analogue $[\ce{Fe(H2O)6}]^{2+}$ (weak field, $sp^3d^2$) has four unpaired electrons and is paramagnetic with $\mu=4.9$ B.M. — the classic comparison that shows the effect of ligand field strength.

questions.question: Draw the structures of the following compounds: (a) 1-ethoxypropane (b) 4-methylpent-3-en-2-one (c) 3-bromo-4-phenylpentanoic acid (d) o-Toluidine (e) m-kresol
questions.answer:
**(a) 1-Ethoxypropane** — an ethyl ether on the first carbon of a propane chain:

$$\ce{CH3CH2-O-CH2CH2CH3}$$

(an unsymmetrical ether, made by Williamson synthesis from sodium ethoxide + 1-bromopropane).

**(b) 4-Methylpent-3-en-2-one** — a ketone at C-2, double bond C-3=C-4, methyl on C-4; this is **mesityl oxide**, the dehydration product of diacetone alcohol:

$$\ce{CH3-CO-CH=C(CH3)-CH3}$$

**(c) 3-Bromo-4-phenylpentanoic acid** — a five-carbon acid with Br at C-3 and phenyl at C-4:

$$\ce{HOOC-CH2-CH(Br)-CH(C6H5)-CH3}$$

**(d) o-Toluidine** — 2-methylaniline: a benzene ring with $\ce{-NH2}$ at C-1 and $\ce{-CH3}$ at C-2 (ortho):

$$\ce{2-CH3C6H4NH2}$$

**(e) m-Kresol** — 3-methylphenol: a benzene ring with $\ce{-OH}$ at C-1 and $\ce{-CH3}$ at C-3 (meta):

$$\ce{3-CH3C6H4OH}$$

(isomeric with o- and p-cresol; all three occur in coal tar).

questions.question: Write short notes on the following: (a) Cannizzaro reaction (b) Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction (c) Carbylamine reaction.
questions.answer:
**(a) Cannizzaro reaction.** Aldehydes that have **no $\alpha$-hydrogen** undergo **disproportionation** in concentrated alkali — one molecule is oxidised to the carboxylate salt, another reduced to the alcohol:

$$\ce{2HCHO + NaOH -> HCOONa + CH3OH}$$

$$\ce{2C6H5CHO + NaOH -> C6H5COONa + C6H5CH2OH}$$

A hydride is transferred from the hydrate anion of one molecule to the carbonyl carbon of the other. Because there is no $\alpha$-H, the competing aldol condensation cannot occur.

**(b) Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction.** A carboxylic acid with an **$\alpha$-hydrogen** is brominated at the $\alpha$-carbon using **Br$_2$ and a catalytic amount of red phosphorus**:

$$\ce{R-CH2COOH + Br2 ->[P] R-CH(Br)COOH + HBr}$$

The phosphorus converts some acid to the acid bromide, which enolises readily and reacts with Br$_2$; the $\alpha$-bromo acid is a key intermediate for $\alpha$-amino acids and $\alpha$-hydroxy acids.

**(c) Carbylamine reaction.** **Primary** amines, aliphatic or aromatic, on warming with **chloroform and alcoholic KOH** give the foul-smelling **isocyanide**:

$$\ce{RNH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH ->[\Delta] RNC + 3KCl + 3H2O}$$

$$\ce{C6H5NH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH -> C6H5NC + 3KCl + 3H2O}$$

It is the standard **test for a primary amine**: secondary and tertiary amines, having no replaceable hydrogens on nitrogen, give no isocyanide, so the test also distinguishes the classes of amine.
